Hook: In 1982 Peter Diamond imagined an island. Coconuts grow on tall palm trees, and climbing one is hard work. A taboo forbids eating a coconut you picked yourself. You may only eat one you trade for. So climbing is worth the effort only if you expect to meet someone else who has climbed, someone to trade with.

Draw it. Along the bottom, the share of islanders you expect to be climbing. Up the side, the share for whom climbing then pays. If few climb, partners are scarce, and climbing does not pay. If most climb, partners are easy to find, and it does. Where the curve meets the diagonal, expectations are self-fulfilling: nobody climbs; or almost everyone does; with an unstable point in between. The same island, the same people, the same trees, and either a slump or a boom. Diamond shared the Nobel prize in 2010 with Dale Mortensen and Christopher Pissarides, for the theory of markets where people must search for each other.

Real labour markets look like that island. In the latest American figures, firms were advertising about 7.5 million job openings. At the same time, about 7.1 million people were unemployed and looking for work. In a frictionless market of Part two's kind, one of those numbers would be zero: the price would clear the market. Here both are large at once, every month.

This part's question: why are there unemployed workers and unfilled jobs at the same time? How should someone looking for work decide which offer to take? How do workers and jobs meet, and what sets the wage when they do? And why does unemployment swing so much more than the theory says it should?
Economics, Built. Part twenty-four: looking for work.

This part closes Act Five. You'll see how many jobs begin and end in a quiet month. You'll play a search game and compare your stopping rule with the best one. You'll draw the Beveridge curve from American data, estimate the matching function, and derive the model that central banks use for the labour market. Then how wages are bargained, when the market creates the right number of jobs, and why the model's unemployment barely moves. And what drives unemployment over the cycle, how workers climb job ladders, the natural rate, two dials, and the new data from job boards.
Flows: Every month, the American Bureau of Labor Statistics asks a large sample of employers how many people they hired, and how many left. The survey began at the end of 2000. In an ordinary month before the pandemic, employers hired about 5.0 million people. And about 4.9 million left their jobs: more than half of them, about 2.6 million, because they quit; the rest were laid off, or left for other reasons, such as retirement. The difference, close to the change in payroll jobs that the news reports each month, was only about 84 thousand. In April 2020, separations jumped to 11.5 million in a single month.

So think of unemployment as water in a tub. The level is a stock: the share of the labour force that is out of work and looking. Water flows in when people who have jobs lose or leave them: a fraction s of the employed, each month. And it drains out when the unemployed find work: a fraction f of them. The level rises if the inflow exceeds the outflow, and falls if not. Every model in this part is a theory of s and f.

When the tub settles, inflow equals outflow. s times one minus u equals f times u, so the steady-state rate is s over s plus f. Chapter ten measures these flows for America since 1948. On average, about 55 percent of the unemployed found work each month, and about 3 percent of the employed lost or left their jobs into unemployment. That gives about 5.4 percent, close to the average unemployment rate. The flows are so fast that the level never strays far from its steady state for long. Steven Davis and John Haltiwanger found the same churn among employers, using the records of manufacturing plants: in every industry and every year, the jobs created and destroyed dwarf the net change. A market where so much is always moving needs a theory of how workers and jobs meet.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: take it, or keep looking?

Your turn. You are out of work, and one job offer arrives each month. Each offer is a monthly wage somewhere between 50 and 150, every value equally likely. While you look, you receive an unemployment benefit of 40 a month. A job you accept, you keep for ever, and you cannot go back to an offer you turned down. And you are a little impatient: next month's money is worth 0.95 of this month's. Choose your rule before the offers arrive. You will take the first offer of at least: A, eighty; B, a hundred; C, a hundred and twenty; or D, a hundred and forty. Pause, and choose.

Here come the offers. Eighty-eight; seventy-one; a hundred and four; sixty-three; ninety-seven; a hundred and twenty-one; seventy-nine; a hundred and thirty-five; ninety-two; a hundred and ten. Now your rule. A, eighty, stops at once: eighty-eight, in the first month. B, a hundred, takes a hundred and four in the third month. C, a hundred and twenty, waits until the sixth month and takes a hundred and twenty-one. And D, a hundred and forty, never stops: after ten months it is still looking, still living on the benefit. In hindsight, the best offer was a hundred and thirty-five, in month eight. But nobody searching knows which offer is the best one until it is too late.

How did you do? Score each rule by the present value of everything it brings, benefits while searching and the wage for ever after. On these particular offers, C did best. But luck matters in any single draw, so the right score is the value a rule is expected to bring before the offers are seen. A, too eager, is worth a job paying about a hundred and ten for ever. B, about a hundred and seventeen. C, about a hundred and twenty-one. D, too choosy, about a hundred and nine: it waits ten months, on average, for an offer that good. The best possible rule, worked out in the next chapter, takes the first offer of at least 120.9. If you chose C, you were almost exactly right.
Search: Chapter three. Search: the reservation wage.

The economics of looking begins with George Stigler in 1961. Prices for the same thing differ from shop to shop, he observed, and finding the low one takes time. His searcher decides in advance how many shops to visit, then buys at the cheapest. In 1970 John McCall turned it into the problem you just played: decide after each offer whether to stop. In both, the spread of prices or wages, and the time spent unemployed, are not mistakes. They are what looking costs, chosen by people doing the best they can.

Here is the best rule. A job at wage w, kept for ever, is worth w this month, beta w next month, and so on: w over one minus beta. Looking is worth the benefit now, plus, discounted, the better of two things next month: the job you are offered, or looking on. Since a job's value rises with its wage and looking's does not, there is a wage w star at which you are indifferent: the reservation wage. Take any offer above it, refuse any below. Rearranging gives its condition. On the left, what one more month of looking costs: the reservation wage you could have had, less the benefit. On the right, what it gains: the expected amount by which next month's offer beats the reservation wage, valued for ever. Stop when the two are equal.

Draw both sides. The cost of looking on rises one for one with the reservation wage. The expected gain from one more offer falls: the choosier you already are, the less likely another offer is to beat your standard, and the less it beats it by. They cross at 120.9, the rule from the game. About 29 percent of offers clear it, so a searcher expects to look for about 3.4 months. That time is unemployment, and none of it is a mistake.

What moves the rule? A bigger benefit makes looking cheaper, so the searcher holds out for more: with no benefit at all, searchers on the Island accept anything above 115, and with a benefit of a hundred and twenty, only offers above 137. Expected search more than doubles, from 2.9 months to 7.5. Patience works the same way. A searcher who discounts next month heavily takes almost anything; one who barely discounts it waits for the top of the distribution. So unemployment insurance has a cost, in longer spells, as well as a benefit, in better matches and in protecting people who lose their jobs. How big is the cost?

The evidence agrees with the sign. Lawrence Katz and Bruce Meyer used the records of unemployment insurance in twelve American states. They found that one more week of potential benefits lengthened spells by about a sixth to a fifth of a week. David Card, Raj Chetty and Andrea Weber studied more than half a million job losers in Austria, where severance pay depends sharply on tenure. Workers who received a payment worth two months of earnings found jobs more slowly. A lump sum does not change the reward for taking a job, so that is not the incentive at work: it is cash. Workers with money in hand can afford to wait for a better offer, the same lesson as Part twenty-two's households. How to design insurance with both effects in mind waits for Part forty-two.
Beveridge: In 1944 William Beveridge, the architect of Britain's welfare state, defined full employment as having more vacant jobs than unemployed people. Plot the two against each other. Along the bottom, the American unemployment rate; up the side, job openings as a share of all jobs, filled or not, month by month since the end of 2000. In the 2000s the points trace a downward-sloping curve: when openings are plentiful, unemployment is low. The recession of 2008 slides the economy down and to the right. The slow recovery of the 2010s climbs back up, but to the right of the old curve: for the same openings, more unemployment. Then the pandemic: unemployment leaps to almost fifteen percent in a single month, and comes back fast. And from mid 2021, openings soar to levels never recorded, with unemployment below four percent. The latest point, 2026-09: unemployment 4.2 percent, openings 4.4.

Chapter six builds the model that explains the curve. Here is what it says, in advance. When productivity rises and falls, firms post more or fewer vacancies, and the economy slides along a downward-sloping curve. A boom moves it up and to the left; a slump, down and to the right. But if workers and jobs find each other less efficiently, or if more matches break up, the whole curve moves outward: more unemployment and more vacancies at the same time. Why the American curve moved out after 2009 is still argued: a mismatch between the skills and places of the unemployed and the jobs on offer; extended unemployment benefits; or firms recruiting less intensively for each opening. Bart Hobijn and Ayşegül Şahin, and Michael Elsby, Ryan Michaels and David Ratner, survey the debate.

The curve became a forecasting argument in 2022. In 2022, there were almost two openings for every unemployed worker, and inflation was the highest in forty years. Could the Federal Reserve cool the labour market without a big rise in unemployment? Olivier Blanchard, Alex Domash and Lawrence Summers argued no: the curve was flat, so fewer openings would mean many more unemployed. Andrew Figura and Christopher Waller, at the Federal Reserve, replied that the curve is steep when openings are so plentiful: firms could cut vacancies with few lost jobs. Since then, openings have fallen most of the way back while unemployment has risen by well under a point: so far, closer to Figura and Waller.

One of the series' facts. In the data, openings and unemployment move in opposite directions along a curve that sometimes shifts. In theory, the curve is where the flows into and out of unemployment balance, with job finding rising in openings per searcher. And Agora's Island, which chapter six builds, has both at once in a perfectly steady state.
Matching: Why don't searchers and openings simply pair off? Here is the simplest answer, from Gerard Butters and Robert Hall in the 1970s. Twelve openings, and twelve people looking for work. Each applies to one opening, chosen at random, because nobody knows where the others are applying. Watch. Only 8 openings are filled. 4 received no applicant at all, while 4 received more than one and could hire only one. Nobody was lazy or choosy; they just failed to coordinate. On average, with U searchers and V openings, the number of hires is V times one minus e to the minus U over V: here about 7.8 out of twelve. A missing price is not the problem. Missing information is.

Economists summarize all this with a matching function. The number of hires each month depends on the number of searchers and the number of openings. Usually it is written as a Cobb-Douglas with constant returns: double both, and hires double. Then everything depends on one ratio, openings per searcher, called the market's tightness, theta. A searcher finds a job at rate f, which rises with tightness; a vacancy is filled at rate q, which falls with it. In a tight market, workers find jobs easily and firms struggle to fill them; in a slack market, the reverse. And every new searcher makes it slightly harder for the others, every new vacancy slightly harder for other firms: an externality that chapter eight returns to.

Can the matching function be seen in data? Take logs: the log of the job-finding rate is a constant plus one minus eta times the log of tightness. Here are the American quarters from 2001 to 2019: the share of the unemployed who found work, which chapter ten measures, against openings per unemployed worker. The slope is 0.42, so the elasticity of hires with respect to unemployment, eta, is about 0.58. Using JOLTS's count of all hires instead gives a slope of 0.69, but those hires include people moving from one job to another, who are not in the unemployment pool. Which measure of searchers to use is a large part of this literature. Barbara Petrongolo and Christopher Pissarides surveyed dozens of estimates in 2001: constant returns hold up well, and the elasticity on unemployment is usually between a half and seven-tenths. That number is a dial in chapter thirteen.
DMP: Now the model that Peter Diamond, Dale Mortensen and Christopher Pissarides built in the 1980s, the one central banks still use for the labour market. Start with firms. A firm may open a vacancy, at a cost c each month it stays open. It is filled at rate q of theta, which falls as the market gets tighter. The value of the vacancy, times the interest rate, is the cost this month plus the chance of filling it times what a filled job is worth. A filled job produces p a month, pays the wage w, and breaks up at rate s. Its value is the profit flow over r plus s. Anyone may open a vacancy, so firms keep opening them until one more is worth nothing. Then the expected cost of hiring, c over q, the cost per month times the expected months to fill it, equals the value of the worker hired. That is the job-creation condition.

Draw it. Across the bottom, tightness; up the side, the wage. Job creation slopes down: the tighter the market, the longer a vacancy takes to fill, so the dearer hiring is, and the lower the wage at which it still pays to open one. The wage curve slopes up: the wage is bargained, as the next chapter derives, and in a tight market a worker who walks away finds another job sooner, so the worker can ask for more. Where they cross, the Island's labour market settles: about 1.8 vacancies for every unemployed worker, and a wage of 0.977 out of output of one. These are the Island's planted parameters: benefits worth four-tenths of output, a three percent chance each month that a job ends, and the cost of keeping a vacancy open.

Now bring back chapter one's tub. Unemployment is steady when separations equal job finding, and job finding depends on vacancies per unemployed worker. Every pair of unemployment and vacancies that balances the flows lies on a downward-sloping curve: the model's Beveridge curve. The last picture fixed tightness, the ratio of vacancies to unemployment: a ray from the origin. Where the ray crosses the curve, the Island has 3.5 percent unemployment and 6.6 percent vacancies at the same time, for ever, in a perfectly steady economy. Each month about 82 percent of the unemployed find jobs, and each vacancy has about a 44 percent chance of being filled. That answers the part's question, in one model: both exist at once because finding each other takes time.

What happens in a slump? Suppose productivity falls three percent, for good. Vacancies can be opened or closed overnight, so tightness jumps at once to its new level: from 1.85 to 1.75. Unemployment is a stock, so it follows more slowly, at the rate s plus f: half the way in under a month, because the flows are so fast. And look at the scale. A three percent fall in productivity, large by the standards of the business cycle, raises the Island's unemployment by less than a tenth of a point. In a real recession, American unemployment rises by several points. Hold on to that; it is chapter nine's puzzle.
Bargaining: Chapter seven. Nash bargaining and the split of the surplus.

In the Beveridge picture there is no auctioneer. So what sets the wage? Once a worker and a firm have found each other, both are better off together than apart: walking away means searching again. The match creates a surplus, the worker's gain over staying unemployed plus the firm's gain over an empty vacancy. Any wage that leaves both gains positive would be accepted. Nothing in the market picks one. The model uses John Nash's bargaining solution: the wage that maximizes the product of the two gains, weighted by beta and one minus beta. The worker ends up with a share beta of the surplus. Ariel Rubinstein's game of alternating offers, from Part eleven, gives the same split when offers come quickly, with beta reflecting how patient each side is.

Work out the share, and the wage comes out simply. It is a weighted average: one minus beta times the benefit the worker would get while unemployed, plus beta times what the worker is worth to the firm. What the worker is worth includes output, p, and something more: c times theta. In a tight market, a firm that lets this worker go faces a long, costly search for another, and the worker captures part of that saving. That is why the wage curve slopes up. On the Island, half of four-tenths, plus half of one plus 0.3 times 1.85: 0.977. Substitute the wage into job creation and the whole model collapses to one equation in tightness. On the left, the expected cost of a hire plus the worker's share of the search cost saved; on the right, the firm's share of the gap between output and the benefit. Every comparative static in this part comes from this line.

Now move the dials, one at a time, from the Island's 3.5 percent. Raise the benefit from four-tenths to a half: the worker's fallback improves, the wage rises, firms open fewer vacancies, and unemployment rises to 3.9 percent. Raise productivity by five percent: output rises by more than the wage, so firms open more vacancies, and unemployment falls to 3.4. Make jobs half again as likely to end: the tub leaks faster, and unemployment rises to 5.3, even though tightness hardly moves. Give workers a bigger share of the surplus: each hire is worth less to firms, and unemployment rises to 4.3. Notice which change moves unemployment least: productivity, the shock that most theories of the business cycle rely on.

Here is the first of those in the picture. A higher benefit shifts the wage curve up. The crossing slides left: tightness falls from 1.85 to 1.53. And the wage barely rises, from 0.977 to 0.979. Because job creation is nearly flat, a tiny change in the wage moves tightness a lot. That flatness is what the profit margin, p minus w, controls, and it will decide the puzzle in chapter nine.
Hosios: Chapter eight. Efficiency: the Hosios condition.

Does this market create the right number of jobs? Think about one more vacancy. When a firm opens it, two things happen to other people. The unemployed find work a little faster. And other firms fill their own vacancies a little more slowly: congestion. The firm counts neither. It counts only the share of the match surplus it will keep, one minus beta. If workers' share is small, firms keep a lot, and they open too many vacancies that get in each other's way. If workers' share is large, firms open too few, and too many people wait unemployed. Somewhere between, the two effects cancel.

Score the Island's market by what it produces, net of what it spends on searching: output from everyone employed, plus what the unemployed produce at home, which the benefit stands for, minus the cost of all the open vacancies. Now vary the worker's bargaining share, and solve the model again for each. Net output is highest when the share is 0.50. That is exactly the elasticity of matches with respect to unemployment, eta, in the Island's matching function. Arthur Hosios proved in 1990 that this is no coincidence: with constant returns in matching, the decentralized market is efficient exactly when workers' share of the surplus equals their share in producing matches. Nothing guarantees that bargaining delivers it.

Hosios's result needs constant returns in matching. Diamond's island does not have them. There, the more people climb, the easier each one finds a trading partner: a thick-market externality, with increasing returns. That is why it has several equilibria, and why the one where nobody climbs is a coordination failure. A slump that nobody chose, and that everyone's pessimism sustains: Russell Cooper and Andrew John showed in 1988 how many macroeconomic models share this structure. The estimates in chapter five find roughly constant returns in real labour markets, so most economists treat Diamond's slump as a possibility to keep in mind, not as the ordinary state of things.
Volatility: Chapter six ended with a warning. Here is the data that makes it a puzzle. Take each quarter from 2001 to 2019 and strip out the slow trends, leaving the business cycle. Openings per unemployed worker swing enormously: in the Great Recession they fell to well under half their trend. Their standard deviation is about 0.39. Output per hour, the productivity that drives the model, barely moves: a standard deviation of about 1.6 percent. Tightness is about 25 times as volatile as productivity. Robert Shimer made the same comparison in 2005, for 1951 to 2003, with older data on help-wanted advertising: almost twenty times.

Now ask the model the same question: when productivity rises one percent, by how much does tightness rise? The data say about 25. Shimer calibrated the model to American averages: benefits worth four-tenths of output, a worker's share and a matching elasticity of 0.72. It answers 1.7. The reason is the wage. When productivity rises, Nash bargaining hands most of the gain to the worker, through both p and the tighter market, so the profit from a new hire hardly changes, and firms open hardly any more vacancies. In 2008 Marcus Hagedorn and Iourii Manovskii proposed different numbers: a fallback worth ninety-five percent of output, and a worker's share of five percent. Then the model answers 34: more than enough.

Called it? In 1994 Dale Mortensen and Christopher Pissarides simulated their model, driven by aggregate shocks alone, and reported that it reproduced reasonably well the cyclical behaviour of job creation and job destruction in the United States. The pattern held up: in recessions job destruction jumps and job creation falls, as their model says. The size did not. Shimer showed that with productivity shocks of the size actually observed, the model's vacancies and unemployment barely move. Robert Hall put it the same way: the model explains the direction of the labour market's response to shocks, but needs implausibly large shocks to explain the magnitude. Partly right.

Twenty years of repairs followed. Robert Hall's answer was sticky wages: if the wage does not rise with productivity, the whole gain is profit, and firms rush to hire. But Christopher Pissarides pointed out in 2009 that what matters for opening a vacancy is the wage of the person hired, and the wages of new hires move strongly with the cycle in the studies he reviewed, even when the wages of long-standing employees do not. Hall and Paul Milgrom replaced Nash's threat of walking away with Rubinstein's alternating offers, so that the outside market matters less to the wage. Hagedorn and Manovskii's small surplus works, but it says that the unemployed are almost as well off as the employed. And other work looks for shocks other than productivity: to the rate at which firms discount the future, to credit, to demand.

In 2017 Lars Ljungqvist and Thomas Sargent showed what all these repairs have in common. The elasticity of tightness with respect to productivity factors into two pieces. The first is always between one and one over eta: it cannot do much. The second is output divided by output minus the worker's fallback: one over what they call the fundamental surplus. Every repair that works shrinks the fundamental surplus. With Shimer's numbers, one over one minus 0.4 is about 1.7, and the elasticity is 1.7. With Hagedorn and Manovskii's, it is about 22, and the elasticity is 34. So the puzzle becomes a question of measurement: how much of a job's output is left over after paying what the worker could get elsewhere? If little, small shocks move unemployment a lot.
InsOuts: Chapter one's tub has two pipes. When unemployment rises, which one changed? To answer, you need the flows, and before JOLTS there were none. Robert Shimer found them in a number the Current Population Survey has published since 1948: how many of the unemployed have been looking for less than five weeks. Next month's unemployed are this month's, less those who found work, plus those who just became unemployed. So the share who found work, F, can be read off. Convert it to a rate, f, allowing for people who find and lose jobs within the same month, and back out the separation rate from the change in the stock. One wrinkle: the survey was redesigned in 1994 and now counts fewer people as newly unemployed; Agora scales the short-term count by 1.1 from then on, a correction in the spirit of Shimer's.

Here are the two rates, quarter by quarter, since 1948. Job finding averages about 55 percent a month, and it collapses in every recession: in 2010 it fell below a quarter. Separation averages about 3.2 percent a month. It jumps at the start of recessions, but briefly, and with much smaller swings in proportion. The spring of 2020 is the exception: more than twenty million payroll jobs lost in April alone, most of them temporary layoffs: a burst of separations unlike anything before.

Now split unemployment's swings between the two. In white, the steady-state rate the two flows imply each quarter, which tracks actual unemployment closely. In green, what it would have been if only job finding had moved, with separation held at its average. In red, if only separation had moved. Green follows white far more closely. Measured by the covariances, job finding accounts for about 72 percent of the variation in unemployment since 1948, and separation for about 28. Shimer found three-quarters and one quarter. Michael Elsby, Ryan Michaels and Gary Solon answered that the inflow still matters, especially at the start of recessions, when layoffs surge before hiring dries up. Both are right about something: recessions begin with job losses and last because hiring stops. That is why the DMP model's focus on job creation is a good place to start, and why its weak amplification is a real problem.
Ladder: Chapter eleven. Job ladders and wage dispersion.

McCall's searcher stops for good at the first acceptable offer. Real careers do not. Robert Topel and Michael Ward followed about ten thousand young American men through the social security records of their employers. A typical young man held seven jobs in his first ten years at work, about two-thirds of all the jobs he would ever hold. And the raises he got when he changed jobs accounted for at least a third of his wage growth early in his career. Search does not end with the first job. People keep looking while they work, and climb.

Here is one simulated career on the Island's job ladder. Offers arrive now and then, whether you are employed or not: about one month in ten. The rule is simple. If you are unemployed, take any offer, since every firm pays at least the benefit. If you are employed, take any offer that beats your current wage. Each move is a step up. And now and then the job ends, and you drop back to the bottom and start again. A career is a staircase with occasional falls.

Kenneth Burdett and Dale Mortensen asked what wages firms would choose to pay on such a ladder. Every worker is the same and every firm is the same, yet in equilibrium firms do not all pay the same wage. A firm that pays more makes less on each worker, but recruits more of them, and loses fewer to rivals. A firm that pays less keeps a fatter margin on a smaller, leakier workforce. Profits are equal along the whole range of wages. On the Island, offers spread from 0.40, the benefit, up to 0.98. The wages people actually earn are higher than the wages offered, because workers keep climbing: on average 0.90 against 0.76. And firms that pay more are bigger: the link between wages and employer size that the data show everywhere.

There is a deeper lesson here. In a market without frictions, a firm that cut its wage by a cent would lose every worker at once. On a job ladder, it loses some, gradually, as they find better offers, and it recruits a little more slowly. Each firm faces a supply of labour that slopes upward. That is a kind of monopsony power, and it exists even with many employers, because finding them takes time. Alan Manning built a book around this idea in 2003. Its evidence, and what it implies for the minimum wage, are Part thirty-eight's.
Natural: Chapter twelve. The natural rate, duration and scarring.

Every model in this part has a steady state: a rate of unemployment that the flows return to when the shocks die away. Milton Friedman called it the natural rate in 1968. Nothing about it is natural in the sense of good or fixed: it depends on how fast people separate and find jobs. Here is American unemployment since 1949. And the Congressional Budget Office's estimate of the natural rate, which it uses to judge how far the economy is from capacity. It peaked at about 6.2 percent in the late 1970s and has drifted down to about 4.4. Among the explanations: an older and more educated workforce, which separates less; temporary-help agencies and better matching; and perhaps online search. Part twenty-eight returns to the natural rate as a guide for central banks, where estimating it in real time turns out to be hard.

Averages hide who is unemployed for how long. This is the share of the unemployed who have been looking for more than six months. Before 2008 it never passed about a quarter, reached in the slump of the early 1980s. After the 2008 crisis it reached about 46 percent in 2010: almost half of all unemployed Americans had been looking for more than half a year, because job finding stayed low for years. That raises a hard question. Do people who have been unemployed longer find jobs more slowly because of the spell itself, or because the people who are hardest to employ are the ones left in the pool?

Kory Kroft, Fabian Lange and Matthew Notowidigdo answered with an experiment. They sent fictitious résumés to real job postings in a hundred American cities. The résumés were alike except for one thing, assigned at random: how long the applicant had been out of work. The chance of being called back for an interview fell from about seven percent to about four as the spell lengthened, with most of the fall within the first eight months. And it fell faster where the labour market was tight, where a long spell is more of a warning sign, since jobs are easy to find. So employers do hold the spell itself against people. The pool is not just sorted; it is shaped by how long people have been in it.

Losing a job leaves a scar. Steven Davis and Till von Wachter used Social Security earnings records from 1974 on, for men who had held their jobs for at least three years and lost them in mass layoffs, which are less likely to reflect the worker's own performance. Displaced when unemployment was below six percent, a man lost, over the next twenty years and discounted, about 1.4 years of his earlier earnings. Displaced when unemployment was above eight percent, about 2.8 years: twice as much. Recessions do not just delay careers; they knock people down the ladder. And when Davis and von Wachter put the same question to the Mortensen-Pissarides model, extended to allow search on the job, it produced losses only about a quarter as large. Another gap between the model and the data.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: the matching elasticity, and the worker's share.

Two dials. The first is the matching elasticity, eta. Petrongolo and Pissarides's survey puts it between a half and seven-tenths. Shimer's regression on half a century of American data gives 0.72. This film's estimate from chapter five, the unemployed's job-finding rate against openings, gives 0.58. Counting all hires, including people moving between jobs, gives 0.31, a reminder that the answer depends on who you count as searching. The status: settled within a range. It matters twice: for how much unemployment responds to openings, and, by Hosios's condition, for how big workers' share should be.

The second dial is the worker's share of the surplus, beta, and it is much less settled. Shimer set it at 0.72, equal to the matching elasticity, so that the market is efficient. Hagedorn and Manovskii set it at 0.05, with a fallback worth ninety-five percent of output, to make unemployment volatile. Pierre Cahuc, Fabien Postel-Vinay and Jean-Marc Robin estimated a model in which employers also compete for workers who search on the job, on French data, and found no significant bargaining power for low- and intermediate-skill workers: what they earn above their fallback comes from competition between employers. The status: contested. The share cannot be read off wages without knowing what the alternative to working is worth, which is the same quantity that decides the volatility puzzle.
